one_liner: Thomas Mueller's Java RecSplit minimal perfect hash: about 2 bits/key, lookups ~1.1x faster than CHD in one code comment.
what_it_does: Builds a minimal perfect hash function (MPHF) over a fixed set of unique keys. Each of the n keys maps to a distinct int in [0, n), and the keys themselves are not stored. You call RecSplitBuilder.newInstance(UniversalHash<T>).leafSize(..).averageBucketSize(..).generate(Collection<T>) to get a BitBuffer (serialize it with toByteArray()), then buildEvaluator(buffer).evaluate(key) returns the slot. It is not a map and not a drop-in for Sux4J's CHD/GOV classes: you keep values in your own array indexed by the result, and the repo also ships an evaluation-only C port (rec-split.c).
how_it_is_fast: It implements RecSplit (Esposito, Mueller Graf, Vigna, arXiv 1910.06416): keys are hashed into buckets, and each bucket is split recursively by brute-force searching for a seed that divides it into the fanout given by precomputed split rules, down to leaves of at most leafSize keys, where a seed giving a bijection is searched. The seeds are stored Golomb-Rice coded, with per-bucket key counts and bit offsets in Elias-Fano monotone lists with select. A lookup is one universal hash, two Elias-Fano reads and a walk down the Rice-coded tree that decodes and skips sibling subtrees; it uses a cheap SplitMix-style supplemental mixer plus Lemire multiply-shift range reduction and calls the full hash only once per 2^18 seeds. Buckets are independent, so construction runs in parallel on a ForkJoinPool, and buckets over 8x the average fall back to a BDZ function (~3.66 bits/key); the main gain over CHD is space (the README claims under 1.58 bits/key is possible) rather than lookup speed.
when_to_use: Static JVM key sets from about 10^5 up to about 10^9 keys where memory per key matters more than lookup latency, e.g. mapping keys to slots in a bitmap or counter array (the use cases in recsplit.md).
You want a pure-Java MPHF under 2 bits/key under Apache-2.0 rather than LGPL-2.1 (Sux4J's license), and you can vendor the source.
Construction time matters on a multi-core box: buckets are built in parallel by default (parallelism = availableProcessors).
Key sets that barely fit in heap: maxChunkSize builds one range of buckets per pass over the collection, as LargeSetTest does for 10^9 longs with 100M-key chunks.
Long or String keys (SipHash-based LongHash/StringHash are included), or any type for which you write a seeded UniversalHash<T>.
when_not_to_use: Lookup throughput is the goal. The author says java.util.HashMap get() being about 8x faster than evaluate() is expected (issue #15). In the same benchmark comment, Sux4J GOV is faster at equal space (132 vs 138 ns/key at 2.32 bits/key).
You must reject keys that are not in the set or store values: no keys or fingerprints are kept, so unknown keys return an arbitrary slot (or 0).
The key set changes: any insert or delete means a full rebuild.

You need a supported dependency. There are no releases or Maven Central artifact (the pom is 1.0-SNAPSHOT), the only documentation is the tests (issue #18), the README says 'work in progress', and there have been no code changes since 2019-06.
More than about 10^9 keys, or C/C++ builds: bit offsets and results are int (a 2^31-bit description cap, about 1B keys at 2 bits/key), and the C code only evaluates functions built in Java.

integration.dependencies: none at runtime for the core (JDK only); the pom also declares jmh-core 1.4 at compile scope and junit 4.13.1 for tests
integration.min_toolchain: Java 8 (pom source/target 1.8); C evaluator built with gcc -O3 via its Makefile
integration.platforms: any JVM; the C evaluator loads big-endian files written by the Java builder
integration.thread_safety: not documented. generate() is internally parallel: each call creates a new ForkJoinPool, which is never shut down. After construction, evaluate() only does positional reads on the shared long[], so concurrent lookups look safe by inspection, but no doc or test confirms it.

gotchas: The serialized function does not record its parameters. buildEvaluator must get the same UniversalHash, leafSize, averageBucketSize and eliasFanoMonotoneLists used for generation, and a mismatch is not detected.

The builder accepts leafSize 1-25, but Settings only has split rules for 7-18: sizes 2-6 throw 'No split rules', and 19+ index past the rules table. Split rules are also cached only for set sizes below 10,240 (getSplit throws above that), so averageBucketSize values near or above that fail even though the builder allows up to 65,536.

Keys must be unique. A duplicate can never be separated, so the leaf seed search loops forever instead of failing. The 163 ns/key figure uses FastLongHash, which the source says is 'not recommended to use in the real world'.

MAVEN.md and runjmh.sh point at org.minperf.bloom.* JMH benchmarks that are no longer in the tree. The org.minperf.hem package (a 10^12-key experiment with its own Builder and FastEvaluator, see issue #12) is a separate code path, not the RecSplitBuilder API.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick minperf over Sux4J GOV only if you need a permissive-licensed (Apache-2.0 vs LGPL-2.1) pure-Java MPHF below 2 bits/key and accept unmaintained code; Sux4J is still active (pushed 2026-05) and wins on lookup time in minperf's own comment. For C++, the same algorithm is maintained in Sux's RecSplit, and PTHash or PtrHash give much faster lookups (37-45 ns/key) at about 3 bits/key.
verified_claims_summary: The only numbers are hand-written comments in PerformanceTest.java: RecSplit with the test-only rotate-and-xor FastLongHash (leafSize 11, averageBucketSize 55) reaches 1.97 bits/key and 163 ns/key, against an unnamed CHD (likely Sux4J's Java CHD, or the repo's own test CHD) at 2.25 bits/key and 182 ns/key (about 1.1x), while GOV at 132 ns/key beats both. No JVM, CPU, compiler flags or key count is recorded (the harness defaults to 100,000 random longs and 100 repeats), and there is no run setup for the baselines.
status_note: Abandoned (the last code change was 2019-06, the last commit a 2021-02 dependabot bump, and there are no releases or Maven artifact), but it is Apache-2.0 and the core builder/evaluator is a few dozen JDK-only classes, so you can vendor it if you pin and test it yourself.
